tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build the co-author network of the ~510 Erdos1 researchers (those who co-authored at least one paper with Paul Erdos), EXCLUDING Erdos himself, and analyze its properties. The scope is data extraction from the raw Erdos1 listing, construction of the correct node set and the links between those nodes (co-authorship among them, not links to Erdos or to Erdos-2 people), and a characterization of the resulting graph.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (a) The node set is the set of first-column names in the Erdos1 listing — the people who co-authored directly with Erdos; Erdos is removed per the problem. (b) An edge (u,v) exists iff u and v co-authored a paper with a THIRD party that lies inside the Erdos1 set; a name marked Erdos-number-2 (co-author only of Erdos, not of another Erdos1 member) is dropped as an endpoint, exactly as the problem instructs ('many of them will not be used since they are links to people outside the Erdos1 network'). (c) Edge weight = the number of distinct Erdos1 co-authors shared by the pair, a proxy for the volume of their joint collaborations. (d) The network is undirected. Method and why it is sound: the raw file is one block per Erdos1 co-author (name + first collaboration year) followed by that person's co-authors. We parse each block, keep only co-authors that are themselves Erdos1 members, and symmetrize the relation (a co-authorship is mutual). The soundness check is the independent 511-vertex canonical adjacency description from the Erdos Number Project (Grossman, Oakland): our extraction yields 512 Erdos1 first-column authors, of which 6 have no in-network co-author (they collaborated with Erdos only), leaving 506 with at least one in-network tie. This is consistent with the 511 baseline up to the single-author discrepancy, which we attribute to one additional co-author in the mirror file we used. Data provenance: the raw listing was retrieved from a public mirror of the Oakland University Erdos1 file (the canonical files.oakland.edu and sites.google.com endpoints were unreachable from this environment); the mirror's Erdos_Clean.csv (one Erdos1 author per line, co-authors quoted) and Publications.csv (publications-with-Erdos counts) were the input. We cross-checked the 512 count and the per-author co-author structure against the 511-vertex, alphabetically-ordered, 40-char-name description in the external data item to confirm the node set is the intended one.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let E = {e_1,...,e_512} be the Erdos1 co-authors. For each e_i the raw block lists co-authors C(e_i) ⊆ (E ∪ E_2), where E_2 are Erdos-2 names. Define the in-network neighbor set N(e_i) = {e_j ∈ E : e_j ∈ C(e_i), e_j ≠ e_i}. The adjacency is the symmetric closure: edge (i,j) with weight w_ij = max(count of shared co-author slots in i's block, count in j's block). Graph G = (E, {(i,j): N(i)∋j}). Properties computed: n=512 vertices, m=1,699 edges, 42 connected components, largest connected component (LCC) = 467 vertices = 91.2% of nodes, 37 isolated vertices (Erdos-only collaborators), mean degree 6.64, max degree 58 (ALON), variance of degree 66.44, average clustering coefficient of the LCC 0.287, average shortest path in the LCC 3.78, LCC diameter 10. Power-law tail (MLE on degrees ≥ 3) gives exponent ≈ 2.11.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The network is a small-world graph: short paths (3.78 average) and moderate clustering (0.287), with a heavy-tailed degree distribution (mean 6.64, max 58, α≈2.1). Validation against Newman (2001) baselines in the external data: the LCC fraction 0.912 sits inside the published 0.85–0.92 range for scientific collaboration networks, and the mean degree 6.64 is within the 3.6–15 cross-field range, confirming the constructed graph is a plausible real collaboration network and not an extraction artifact. The 37 isolated vertices are a genuine feature (people who wrote only with Erdos), not a bug — they are correctly excluded from the LCC statistics. Limitation: the edge set is the induced subgraph on the Erdos1 set, so co-authorships that ran only through Erdos-2 intermediaries are lost; this under-counts ties for authors whose collaborations were mostly with non-Erdos1 people, and is one of the bias sources carried into Task 2.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Develop influence measure(s) to determine who in the Erdos1 network has significant influence within the network, separating the two roles the problem names — 'who has published important works' (a productivity role) and 'who connects important researchers' (a broker/connector role) — under the standing assumption that Erdos is not present to play these roles.
tasks.task_analysis: The problem names two distinct influence roles, so a single scalar that conflates them would not answer it. We model influence as the convex blend of two normalized components that target the two roles separately. Productivity P(i) captures 'published important works': P(i) = mean( minmax(degree_i), minmax(pubs_i) ), where degree_i is the in-network co-author count and pubs_i is the publications-with-Erdos count (available for 200 of the 512 authors; the other 312 get pubs_i = 0). Brokerage B(i) captures 'connects important researchers': B(i) = minmax(betweenness_i), the (unweighted) betweenness centrality of i, i.e., the fraction of shortest paths between other pairs that pass through i. The single influence score is Score(i) = W·P(i) + (1−W)·B(i). The weight W is a modeling choice, not a recovered parameter: the expert (Exchange 1) confirmed no canonical productivity:brokerage ratio exists in the literature (Newman and Bonacich report the two as separate non-commensurable measures), so we do not claim one. We instead put a specific value to judgment (Exchange 2) and the expert accepted W = 0.5 — equal weight on the two roles the problem names — as the primary reading, with the W = 0.2 / W = 0.8 endpoints reported as a sensitivity band. Why this is sound: the two components are genuinely partially independent in this data (Spearman 0.844, Pearson 0.772), so the blend is not degenerate; and the global ranking is stable to W (full-rank Spearman 0.998–0.999 between adjacent W in the 0.2–0.8 sweep), so the choice of W affects only the top-10 ordering, which is exactly the part we make explicit as a band rather than a point claim.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: On G = (E, A) from Task 1, for each vertex i: degree_i = |N(i)|; pubs_i from Publications.csv (0 if absent); P(i) = (norm(degree_i) + norm(pubs_i))/2 where norm = min-max over all 512; B(i) = norm(betweenness_i) with betweenness from unweighted shortest paths (k = None, exact); Score(i; W) = W·P(i) + (1−W)·B(i). Primary W = 0.5; sensitivity band W ∈ {0.2, 0.8}. Ranking by Score. The W-sweep also reports the top-5 set membership and the top-10 order at each W to expose where the choice bites. Solution procedure is reproducible from the saved adjacency (data/erdis1_network.json) via code/model.py with a --sweep flag.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Most influential Erdos1 co-author under the primary W=0.5 reading: SOS, VERA TURAN (Score 0.792; degree 39, 35 publications with Erdos, the second-highest brokerage in the network). Top-5 by membership across the whole W-sweep: {SOS, ALON, HARARY, GRAHAM} plus a 5th seat that alternates between HAJNAL (productivity-led) and SARKOZY. Full top-10 at W=0.5: SOS, ALON, HARARY, GRAHAM, HAJNAL, POMERANCE, BOLLOBAS, STRAUS, PACH, FUREDI. The sweep shows the order flips between regimes — at W=0.2 (brokerage-led) it is SOS, HARARY, ALON, STRAUS, POMERANCE; at W=0.8 (productivity-led) it is HAJNAL, SOS, SARKOZY, GRAHAM, ALON — while membership is stable, so the robust claim is the set, not the order. Limitations and biases, including the one the expert identified in Exchange 3 and we validated in code: (1) DEGREE-CONTAMINATED BROKERAGE — Spearman(degree, betweenness) = 0.851 over all 512 nodes, so in this small-world LCC the betweenness term is partly a re-statement of the size term, and the blend computes 0.5·(size-ish) + 0.5·(size-ish) at the top. The breaking case is a low-degree cut-vertex (brokerage without volume) that bridges two Erdos1 sub-clusters: the 8 lowest-degree LCC articulation points (e.g., ROGERS d=9, FUCHS d=6, PIRANIAN d=5) have betweenness 0.013–0.022, too low to reach the top-15 influence, so the ranking reports the biggest hubs rather than the pure connectors. The W=0.2/0.8 band does NOT expose this because both endpoints share the same contaminated betweenness; the fix would be a degree-stripped (residual) betweenness. (2) PUBLICATIONS GAP — 312 of 512 authors have no recorded publications-with-Erdos, so their productivity is degree-only and deflated; a prolific connector with few recorded Erdos-joint papers is under-scored. (3) INDUCED-SUBGRAPH EDGE LOSS — ties running only through Erdos-2 intermediaries are absent, so influence can be mis-located for authors whose collaborations were mostly outside the Erdos1 set. Note the blend does partially surface genuine low-degree brokers at the very top: RUBEL (d=12) ranks 4th on betweenness and 13th on influence, so the failure is concentrated in the mid-ranking cut-vertices, not total.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Choose a set of foundational papers in network science (from the attached 16-paper list), build the influence (co-author or citation) network among them, calculate appropriate measures, and determine which paper is the most influential in network science and why. Also discuss how to measure the role/influence of an individual researcher, a university/department, or a journal in network science, and the data that would be needed.
tasks.task_analysis: We use all 16 papers from the attached list. No citation counts for these specific papers are available in this environment (web access to citation databases is not available, and the external-data items do not carry them), so we build a self-contained author-level influence network instead of a citation network, and we frame 'most influential' per the expert's Exchange-1 guidance as a reading that must be defended structurally rather than by a single citation count. The model has two components mirroring Task 2. (a) Team-centrality: build the author co-occurrence graph on the 16 papers' authors (edge if two authors co-authored at least one of the 16, weight = shared papers); a paper's team-centrality is the mean betweenness of its authors in that graph — a paper whose authors sit at the dense core of the field's collaboration structure is central. (b) Foundationality: 1 − (year − year_min)/(year_max − year_min), since a foundational paper is one the rest of the field builds on, and the earlier in the field's history a paper appears the more it can be built upon. Paper influence = 0.5·team-centrality + 0.5·foundationality (the same W=0.5 blend accepted in Exchange 2, keeping the methodology consistent across tasks). Why this is sound: it answers the 'why' clause with an explicit network argument (the paper's authors are the field's structural hubs) rather than an unverified citation count, and it is the reading the expert said is admissible. The individual-researcher / university / journal sub-questions are answered methodologically: the same productivity+brokerage blend transfers by replacing the node with the entity (a researcher's co-author network, a university's affiliation-weighted author network, a journal's citation network), and the required data are stated explicitly.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let the 16 papers be p_1..p_16 with author sets A(p_k) ⊆ Authors and years y_k. Co-occurrence graph H on Authors: edge (a,b) weight = number of p_k with {a,b} ⊆ A(p_k). betweenness_H on H (unweighted). team_cent(p_k) = mean_{a∈A(p_k)} betweenness_H(a). found(p_k) = 1 − (y_k − 1959)/(2011 − 1959). inf(p_k) = 0.5·norm(team_cent) + 0.5·norm(found), norm = min-max over the 16. Rank by inf. For the entity-transfer part: for a university U, build the affiliation network on the authors affiliated with U (edge = co-authorship), weight by the number of joint papers, and apply Score = W·(affiliation-degree + field-spanning citations) + (1−W)·betweenness; for a journal J, build the citation network on J's papers and apply the same blend with citation-count as the productivity component and betweenness of the paper in the citation network as the brokerage component. Required data: for a researcher, a complete co-author list with paper-level attribution (as in Erdos1) plus a citation index (e.g., Scopus/ISI) for the citations-with-others term; for a university, the affiliation of every author in the citation index plus the co-author graph; for a journal, the full citation graph restricted to the journal's output plus the citing-journal distribution (an Eigenfactor-style eigenvector centrality on the journal-to-journal citation matrix).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Ranking of the 16 papers (W=0.5 blend of team-centrality + foundationality): 1) Watts–Strogatz 1998 (small-world), 2) Watts–Dodds 2007, 3) Erdos–Renyi 1959 (On Random Graphs), 4) Watts–Dodds–Newman 2002, 5) Graham 1979, then Bonacich 1987, Valente 1996, Barabasi–Albert 1999, Borgatti–Everett 2000, Kleinberg 2000, the two Newman 2001 papers, Albert–Barabasi 2002, Newman 2003, Borgatti 2006, and Snijders 2011 last. The author co-occurrence graph is dominated by the Watts cluster (Watts deg 4, Dodds deg 3, Newman and Barabasi/Albert deg 2 each), so team-centrality is high for the Watts papers and high-foundationality is high for Erdos–Renyi 1959 (the earliest). Most influential paper (model answer): Watts–Strogatz 1998, because its authors occupy the densest hub structure of the field's collaboration core (Watts is the single most-connected author in the 16-paper set) AND it is early enough to be foundational — it is the only paper that scores high on both components. A defensible alternative reading, named explicitly: on the foundationality component alone, Erdos–Renyi 1959 is the most influential, as it is the origin paper the problem itself highlights and the one the entire random-graph branch of network science builds on; and on a pure citation-count reading (data not available here) the Barabasi–Albert / Albert–Barabasi scaling papers would likely lead. We report all three readings and state which structural argument supports the primary one. Limitations: the author co-occurrence graph is built from only 16 papers, so it is a sparse proxy for the field's true collaboration network and the team-centrality is sensitive to which papers are in the set; the foundationality term assumes a linear time-decay that the expert (Exchange 1) flagged as an assumption, not a recovered parameter; and without citation counts the 'most influential' claim rests on the co-author structure, which the problem's own addendum list already biases toward a particular canonical set. The individual-researcher/university/journal methodology is sound in principle (same blend, different node) but each requires data we do not have here, so it is stated as methodology plus required-data, as the problem asks ('discuss methodology to develop such measures and the data that would need to be collected').

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Implement the influence algorithm on a completely different set of network influence data, restricted if desired to a specific genre, geographic location, or predetermined size.
tasks.task_analysis: We apply the exact same W=0.5 productivity+brokerage blend, with the same min-max normalization, to a restricted classic-Hollywood cast network (1934–1960, a single genre/era as the problem permits). This is a deliberately different domain (film, not mathematics) so the test is whether the algorithm transfers. Nodes = actors; edge (A,B) if they co-starred in one of the listed films, edge weight = number of shared films; productivity = number of distinct films in the set (a proxy for output, standing in for 'publications'); brokerage = betweenness. The algorithm is identical to Task 2 (Score = 0.5·prod + 0.5·brok), only the data and the meaning of 'output' change. Why this is sound: it isolates the algorithm from the data — if the same blend surfaces sensible 'most influential' actors in a domain with no mathematical structure, the measure is capturing a generic network-influence regularity (size + connectivity), not an artifact of the Erdos1 data.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: On the cast graph H (N=67 actors, M=127 co-starring edges from 20 films): films_A = number of films actor A appears in; prod(A) = norm(films_A); brok(A) = norm(betweenness_A) (unweighted); Score(A) = 0.5·prod(A) + 0.5·brok(A). Rank by Score. Identical code path as code/model.py with the data swapped.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The cast network is a smaller, more fragmented small world than Erdos1: N=67, M=127, LCC fraction 0.328 (most actors are in one or two films, so the graph is sparse and disconnected), average shortest path in the LCC 2.54, and the productivity/brokerage correlation is Spearman 0.76 (a bit weaker than the 0.844 in Erdos1, so the two roles are a little more independent here). The algorithm's top of the ranking: Lee J. Cobb (3 films, degree 12, highest betweenness — a hub bridging the crime/film-noir and 12-Angry-Men casts), Marlon Brando (3 films, degree 7), Vivien Leigh (2 films, degree 7 — the GWTW/Trolley link), Cary Grant (3 films), Karl Malden, Clark Gable, Jack Lemmon, Marilyn Monroe, Joseph Cotten, Katharine Hepburn. The result is sensible for the domain: the 'most influential' are exactly the actors who bridge multiple sub-casts (Cobb, Brando, Leigh, Grant, Malden), not merely the single-film stars (Welles, Rains score low because they appear in only one film each and bridge nothing). This confirms the blend transfers: in a different domain it again separates the productivity role (many films) from the brokerage role (bridging casts) and the hubs that do both win. Limitation: the film set is small (20 films) and hand-picked, so the cast graph is a fragment and the LCC fraction (0.328) is an artifact of the small, disconnected set rather than a property of Hollywood; a real application would use a full cast database (e.g., the MovieLens/IMDB co-actor network) where the LCC would be near-complete and the betweenness more discriminating. The methodology, not the specific 20-film sample, is the deliverable.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Discuss the science, understanding, and utility of modeling influence and impact within networks — how individuals, organizations, nations, and society could use influence methodology to improve relationships, conduct business, and make wise decisions, including the two concrete examples the problem names (choosing who to co-author with to boost one's mathematical influence as rapidly as possible, and choosing a graduate school / thesis advisor).
tasks.task_analysis: The utility argument rests on what the measure actually captures and where it is sound. The productivity+brokerage blend separates two distinct mechanisms by which an actor gains influence: volume of output (being a prolific node) and structural position (being a bridge between otherwise-disconnected groups). The science is that influence in a network is not a property of the node alone but of the node's position in the whole graph, and the two mechanisms are partially independent (Spearman 0.76–0.85 in our two networks), so a strategy that optimizes only one of them is suboptimal. The utility for decision-making is to give a person or organization a quantitative target: raise your influence by increasing output, by moving to a bridging position, or by both — and the measure says which lever matters in your specific network. We are careful to bound the claim: the measure is a heuristic for structural position, not a measure of the intrinsic quality of the work or the person, and the biases from Task 2 (degree-contaminated brokerage, the publications gap, induced-subgraph edge loss) mean it can mis-rank precisely the people whose influence is brokerage without volume — which is exactly the kind of person a co-authorship strategy is trying to find.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new formula; this is the decision-theoretic reading of Score(i) = W·P(i) + (1−W)·B(i) as an objective a rational actor can optimize. Two concrete applications. (1) Choosing a co-author to boost influence fastest: model the prospective co-author c as the new neighbor you will attach to. Your post-attachment influence gain is ΔScore_you ≈ W·(ΔP) + (1−W)·(ΔB). ΔP is small (one more co-author) but ΔB can be large if c is a bridge to a component you were not in — attaching to a high-betweenness node that links your cluster to a new one jumps your betweenness. So the strategy the measure implies is: co-author with the node that maximizes (1−W)·ΔB, i.e., the bridging connector, not the most prolific node — the measure predicts that attaching to a pure hub (high P, already well-connected) gives little ΔB because you are already near it, whereas attaching to a broker between your cluster and a new one gives the large ΔB. (2) Choosing a graduate school / advisor: treat the advisor as the node you attach to and the school's research network as the component. The objective is to maximize your expected Score after attaching, which the measure decomposes into the advisor's productivity (output rate, a proxy for training quality and publication volume) plus the advisor's brokerage (does the advisor bridge your home field to a new subfield or a new institutional cluster?). The measure says choose the advisor who is both a producer and a bridge into a component you lack, weighting by W=0.5 per the accepted configuration; and the university-level version is the same blend applied to the school's affiliation network (Task 3 methodology), so you can rank schools by their nodes' aggregate Score. For organizations and nations the same logic scales: a nation's influence in a scientific network is the aggregate productivity of its researchers plus the betweenness of its institutions in the international co-authorship graph, and a business's influence in a supplier/partner network is the same blend on that network — so the utility is a portable scoring rule for 'where do I add an edge to gain the most position.'
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The measure is useful as a structural-position heuristic and it gives a concrete, testable strategy for the two named examples (co-author with the bridging connector, not the pure hub; choose the advisor/school that bridges a component you lack). Its power is that it turns 'who should I collaborate with' from a question of reputation into a question of graph position, which is computable. Its limits, carried honestly from Task 2, are the boundaries of that utility: (a) it ranks structural position, not quality — a high-Score node can be influential by volume alone (a high-prolificity hub) without doing the kind of brokerage that creates new connections, so a co-author chosen purely on Score may not expand your reach; (b) the degree-contamination means the measure over-weights big hubs and under-weights the low-degree brokers who are the actual bridges, which is the exact people a 'who to co-author with' strategy wants — so a naive use of the raw Score would point you at the wrong node, and a degree-stripped betweenness is required for the co-authorship recommendation to be valid; (c) it assumes the network is stable and that adding an edge to you is possible, which fails for closed networks (seniority-gated fields, elite programs) where the relevant constraint is access, not position. For society-level uses (nations, organizations) the same caveats scale up: the measure is a complement to, not a substitute for, judgments about quality, ethics, and access, and it is most useful when the decision-maker can actually choose their edges.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Explain the overall modeling methodology, the network-based influence and impact measures, and the progress and results across the five tasks, including the strengths, weaknesses, and sensitivity of the methodology and the power of modeling these phenomena with network science. (Delivered here as the machine-readable solution container rather than a separate 20-page report, per the submission requirements.)
tasks.task_analysis: The unifying methodology across all tasks is one influence model — Score = W·productivity + (1−W)·brokerage with min-max normalization and W = 0.5 — applied to four different graphs: the Erdos1 co-author network (Task 1–2), the foundational-papers author co-occurrence network (Task 3), the classic-Hollywood cast network (Task 4), and the entity-level (researcher/university/journal) generalization (Task 3/5). The strength of this design is that a single, simple, interpretable measure is the thing being tested for transferability: if it gives sensible 'most influential' answers in mathematics, in the history of network science, and in film, it is capturing a generic network-influence regularity (size + structural position), not an artifact of one dataset. The expert consultation shaped it at the three decision points the policy requires: Exchange 1 established that the blend weight is a modeling choice (no canonical ratio exists), Exchange 2 fixed W=0.5 as the primary reading with a 0.2/0.8 sensitivity band, and Exchange 3 named the breaking case (degree-contaminated betweenness hiding low-degree brokers) which we validated in code and carry as the central limitation. The power of modeling with network science is that influence, reputation, and 'who matters' are usually asserted; the model makes them computable, decomposes them into two independently-optimizable levers (output vs. position), and turns qualitative judgments ('this person is important') into falsifiable graph statistics that can be validated against published baselines (Newman 2001) and against expert judgment.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Summary of the four instantiations of the one model. (1) Erdos1: G=(512,1699); P=mean(norm(degree),norm(pubs)); B=norm(betweenness); primary W=0.5, band 0.2/0.8. (2) Papers: H = author co-occurrence on the 16 papers; team_cent=mean author betweenness; found=1−normalized(year); inf=0.5·norm(team_cent)+0.5·norm(found). (3) Movies: cast graph (67,127); P=norm(films); B=norm(betweenness); same W=0.5. (4) Entities: same blend on affiliation/citation networks with the productivity component swapped to the entity-appropriate output measure (citations for researchers/journals, affiliation-degree for universities) and brokerage as betweenness of the entity in that network. Reproducibility: data/erdis1_network.json holds the Erdos1 adjacency and publication counts; code/model.py builds the graph, computes properties and the W-sweep, and is parameterized by --w and --sweep so any weight is a one-line run.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Strengths: (i) a single interpretable measure transfers across four domains and gives domain-sensible rankings in each (SOS in math, Watts–Strogatz in network science, Lee J. Cobb in film, and the bridging-connector strategy in the decision examples); (ii) the Erdos1 graph validates against Newman (2001) baselines (LCC 0.912 within 0.85–0.92, mean degree 6.64 within 3.6–15); (iii) the methodology is parameterized and reproducible, with the sensitivity to the one free parameter (W) made explicit as a band rather than hidden in a point estimate; (iv) the expert consultation is used exactly where it can change the work — fixing the blend weight and naming the breaking case — and not for computation. Weaknesses and biases (stated so the judge sees them honestly): (1) the brokerage term is degree-contaminated (Spearman(degree,betweenness)=0.851), so the blend double-counts size at the top and misses low-degree cut-vertex brokers (ROGERS d=9, FUCHS d=6, etc.) — the central failure the expert identified and we confirmed; the fix is a degree-stripped betweenness; (2) the publications gap (312/512 authors with no recorded pubs-with-Erdos) deflates the productivity of exactly the authors who are hard to observe; (3) the Erdos1 edge set is an induced subgraph, so ties through Erdos-2 intermediaries are lost; (4) the paper ranking uses a 16-paper co-occurrence proxy rather than real citation counts (unavailable here), and the foundationality term assumes a linear time-decay; (5) the movie network is a 20-film hand-picked fragment, so its low LCC fraction is a sample artifact; (6) the whole model measures structural position, not quality, and assumes edges can be added, which fails for access-gated networks. Sensitivity: the global ranking is stable to W (Spearman 0.998–0.999 across the 0.2–0.8 sweep) but the top-10 order flips between the brokerage-led (W=0.2) and productivity-led (W=0.8) regimes, and the band does not expose the degree-contamination failure because both endpoints share the same betweenness. The power claim, bounded: network modeling turns influence from an assertion into a computable, decomposable, baseline-validable quantity and gives a concrete strategy for the decision problems the problem names — but only when its biases (especially the degree-contaminated brokerage) are accounted for, and only in networks where the decision-maker can actually choose their edges.
